3.27.m: Nārada said: / From there one should go to the unsurpassed Kanyātīrtha, O knower of dharma. / Bathing at Kanyātīrtha, a person obtains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma.
From there one should go to the excellent place of Brahmā, O tiger among men; / bathing there, a person of lower caste obtains the status of a brāhmaṇa,
while a brāhmaṇa, purified in soul, would go to the supreme state. / From there one should go to the unsurpassed Somatīrtha, O tiger among men.
Bathing there, O king, a person would attain the world of Soma. / From there one should go to the tīrtha Saptasārasvata, O ruler of men,
where Maṅkaṇaka, the world-renowned brahma-seer, attained perfection. / Formerly, O king, Maṅkaṇaka was wounded on the hand by the tip of a kuśa grass blade, so it is renowned;
vegetable sap flowed from his hand, O king. / Seeing that vegetable sap, the great ascetic was filled with joy,
and the brahmin-seer danced, his eyes dilated with astonishment. / Then, when he was dancing, whatever was stationary or moving,
both danced, bewitched by his fiery energy, O hero. / Then by the gods led by Brahmā and by the seers rich in ascetic power,
Mahādeva was petitioned for the sake of the seer, O ruler of men: / “You should act, O god, in such a way that he does not dance.”
Then the god, seeing the sage dancing with a mind overcome by joy, / spoke to him wishing the welfare of the steady [world]:
“Ah, great seer, knower of dharma, why are you dancing? / Why do you have cause for joy today, O best of sages?”
The seer said: / “O best of the twice-born, do you not see that from the wound of me, / an ascetic standing on the path of dharma, vegetable sap has flowed, O holy one?
Seeing that, I have danced, filled with great joy!” / Laughing, the god said to the seer who was bewildered by attachment:
“I, however, do not feel astonishment, O twice-born; look at me here.” / Having spoken thus, O best of men, then by Mahādeva,
O king of kings, his own thumb was struck with the tip of his finger, O sinless one. / From his wound, O king, ash came forth resembling snow.
Seeing this, O king, the sage was ashamed and fell at his feet: / “I consider no other god higher or greater than Rudra.
You are the refuge of the universe of gods and asuras, O trident-holder! / By you this whole universe of three worlds, with the moving and unmoving, was created.
Into you alone, O Lord, all enter at the destruction of the cosmic age. / You cannot be fully known even by the gods; how then by me?
In you, O lord of all, the gods led by Śakra are seen, O sinless one. / You are all; you are the creator and instigator of the worlds day after day.
By your favor all the gods rejoice here, having nothing to fear.” / Having thus praised Mahādeva, the bowed seer said:

"By your grace, O Mahādeva, may my ascetic heat not diminish."
Then the god, delighted in heart, spoke thus to the brāhmanical sage:

"May your ascetic heat increase a thousandfold by my grace, O twice-born.
And I shall dwell here in this hermitage with you, O great sage.

Those who bathe at Saptasārasvata and worship me,
for them nothing is difficult to attain, either in this world or in the next.

And such a one shall go to the world of Sarasvatī; of this there is no doubt."
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva disappeared right there.

Then one should go to Auśanasa, renowned in the three worlds,
where Brahmā and the other gods, as well as ascetics rich in penance,

and the blessed Kārtikeya, O descendant of Bharata, at the three junctions of the day
verily established his presence out of a desire to please the Bhārgava.

Kapālamocana is a sacred ford that destroys all sin.
Bathed there, O tiger among men, one is freed from all sins.

Then one should go to Agnitīrtha; having bathed there, O bull of the Bharatas,
one attains the world of Agni and completely delivers one's family line.

Right there is the sacred ford of Viśvāmitra, O best of the Bharatas.
Having bathed there, O great king, brāhmanahood is attained.

Approaching Brahmayoni, pure and restrained in mind,
having bathed there, O tiger among men, one reaches the world of Brahmā.

And one purifies the family line up to the seventh generation; of this there is no doubt.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the sacred ford renowned in the three worlds,

known as Pṛthūdaka, sacred to Kārtikeya, O king.
There one should take a ceremonial bath, devoted to the worship of ancestors and gods.

Whatever inauspicious deed was done through ignorance or through knowledge,
by a woman or by a man, with human intellect,

all that is destroyed for one the moment one bathes there, O descendant of Bharata;
and one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice, and indeed heaven.

They say Kurukṣetra is sacred; more sacred than Kurukṣetra is the Sarasvatī;
more sacred than the Sarasvatī are its sacred fords, and of sacred fords, Pṛthūdaka.

Whoever casts off his body at Pṛthūdaka, the highest of all sacred fords,
intent on recitation of prayers, shall never again enter the cycle of rebirth.

It was sung by Sanatkumāra and by the great-souled Vyāsa,
and it is ordained in the Veda, O king, that one should visit Pṛthūdaka.

There is no sacred ford more holy than Pṛthūdaka, O best of men;
it is pure, sacred, and purifying; of this there is no doubt.

Having bathed there, even sinful people go to heaven;
thus the wise declare concerning Pṛthūdaka, O best of men.

And right there is the sacred ford Madhusrava, O best of the Bharatas.
Having bathed there, O king, a person obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.

Then one should proceed in due order, O best of men, to the sacred ford of the goddess,
the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the Aruṇā, world-renowned.

Fasting for three nights and bathing there, one is freed from the murder of a brāhmaṇa,
and one obtains the fruit of both the Agniṣṭoma and the Atirātra sacrifices.

And one purifies the family line up to the seventh generation; of this there is no doubt.
And right there, O upholder of the Kuru lineage, is the sacred ford Avakīrṇa,

fashioned long ago by Darbhin out of compassion for the brāhmaṇas.
Whether by vows and investiture, or by fasting, a twice-born,

endowed with rites and mantras, becomes a true brāhmaṇa—of this there is no doubt;
yet even if destitute of rites and mantras, having bathed there, O bull among men,

a twice-born becomes one who has completed his vows; this has been observed from ancient times.
And the four oceans were brought together there by Darbhin.

Having bathed there, O tiger among men, one never meets an evil destiny,
and one obtains the fruits of giving four thousand cows.

Then one should go, O king of kings, to the sacred ford Śatasahasraka,
and Sāhasraka right there—two sacred fords renowned in the world.

Having bathed in both, a person obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows;
and any gift or fast there becomes multiplied a thousandfold.

Then one should go, O king of kings, to the excellent Reṇukātīrtha.
There one should take a ceremonial bath, devoted to the worship of ancestors and gods.

Purified of all sins, he obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma.
Rinsing the mouth at Vimocana, with anger subdued and senses mastered,

one is entirely freed from all sins born of accepting improper gifts.
Then, going to Pañcavaṭa, celibate and self-controlled,

endowed with great merit, one is exalted in the heavenly world,
where Sthāṇu himself, the lord of yoga whose banner is the bull, dwells.

Having worshipped that lord of the gods, one attains perfection merely by going there.
Taijasa, the sacred ford of Varuṇa, shines with its own splendour,

where Guha was consecrated to the generalship of the gods
by the gods headed by Brahmā and by the ascetics rich in penance.

To the east of Taijasa is Kurutīrtha, O upholder of the Kurus.
Having bathed at Kurutīrtha, celibate and self-controlled,

purified of all sins, one reaches the world of Rudra.
Then one should go to Svargadvāra, restrained and taking measured food.

One attains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and goes to the world of Brahmā.
Then, visiting the sacred fords, one should go to Anaraka, O king.

Having bathed there, O king, a person never meets an evil destiny.
There Brahmā himself is constantly exalted alongside the gods.

He presides there, O tiger among men, accompanied by those devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
and his presence is established, O king of kings, upon Rudravedī, O upholder of the Kurus.

Approaching that goddess, one never meets an evil destiny.
And right there, O great king, approaching Viśveśvara, the husband of Umā,

approaching Mahādeva, one is freed from all sins;
and approaching Nārāyaṇa, the lotus-navelled one, O crusher of foes,

radiant, O great king, one reaches the world of Viṣṇu.
Merely by bathing in the sacred fords of all the gods, O king,

freed from all sorrow, one shines forever like Śiva.
Then, visiting the sacred fords, one should go to Asthipura, O king.

Having reached that purifying sacred ford, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the deities;
one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, O descendant of Bharata.

And right there is Gaṅgāhrada and a well, O bull of the Bharatas;
three tens of millions of sacred fords are exalted in that well.

Having bathed there, O king, a man reaches the world of Brahmā.
Having bathed in the Āpagā and worshipped Maheśvara,

one attains the highest state and completely delivers one's family line.
Then one should go to Sthāṇuvaṭa, renowned in the three worlds.

Having bathed there and stayed for a night, one reaches the world of Rudra.
Then one should go to the forest of jujube trees, the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha,

where jujube berries are eaten by a man after fasting for three nights.
He who consumes jujube berries properly for twelve years,

and one who has fasted for three nights, become equal, O king.
Visiting the sacred fords, one should approach Indramārga, O king;

by fasting for a day and a night, one is exalted in the heavenly world.
Approaching Ekarātra, having stayed for one night,

restrained and truthful in speech, one is exalted in the world of Brahmā.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the sacred ford renowned in the three worlds,

where the hermitage of Āditya is, the great-souled mass of splendour.
Having bathed at that sacred ford and worshipped the sun,

one goes to the world of Āditya and completely delivers one's family line.
Visiting the sacred fords, having bathed at Somatīrtha, O upholder of the Kurus,
a man attains the realm of Soma; there is no doubt about this. / Then, O knower of dharma, ruler of men, one should go to Dadhīca's
most holy sacred place, O king, purifying and renowned in the world, / where Sārasvata, that treasure of ascetic heat, attained perfection.
Bathing in that sacred place, a man obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice / and also gains wisdom sacred to Sarasvatī; there is no doubt about this.
Then, having gone to Kanyāśrama, restrained in celibacy, / having stayed for three nights, O king, devoted to fasting,
he obtains a hundred celestial maidens and goes to the world of Brahmā. / Then, O knower of dharma, one should also go to the sacred place Saṃnihitī,
where the gods headed by Brahmā and the sages rich in ascetic heat / assemble month after month, endowed with great merit.
By bathing at Sannihitī when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, / a hundred horse sacrifices have been performed by him eternally.
Whatever sacred places there are on earth and traversing the atmosphere, / and wells, and Brahmins, and holy shrines,
undoubtedly gather on the new-moon day, O ruler of men, / month after month, O tiger among men, lord of the people, at Sannihitī.
Because of the bringing together of sacred places, it is renowned on earth as Sannihitī. / Bathing and drinking there, one is exalted in the heavenly world.
On the new-moon day as well, when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, / listen to the fruit of merit of the mortal who performs a śrāddha there:
Whatever fruit there is of a thousand horse sacrifices duly performed, / that a human being obtains merely by bathing and performing a śrāddha.
Whatever evil deed was done, whether by a woman or by a man, / all of it is destroyed as soon as one has bathed; there is no doubt about this.
In a lotus-colored vehicle he goes to the world of Brahmā. / Then, having saluted by name the gatekeeper Macakruka,
and the pool of Gaṅgā right there, a sacred place, O best of Bharatas, / there the knower of dharma, celibate and concentrated, should bathe.
A human being obtains the fruit of both the Rājasūya and the horse sacrifice. / On earth, Naimiṣa is holy, and in the atmosphere, Puṣkara;
Kurukṣetra is superior even to all three worlds. / Even the dust particles of Kurukṣetra, blown intensely by the wind,
lead even one who has done evil deeds to the supreme destination. / South of the Sarasvatī and north of the Dṛṣadvatī,
those who live in Kurukṣetra live in heaven. / Saying even once the single phrase, 'I will go to Kurukṣetra; I live in Kurukṣetra,'
one is exalted in the heavenly world. / In the sacrificial altar of Brahmā is holy Kurukṣetra, frequented by Brahmin seers;

those who live in it, O king, are not to be pitied in any way. / The region between Taraṇḍa and Kāraṇḍa, and the pools of Rāma, and Macakruka— / this is Kurukṣetra, Samantapañcaka; it is called the northern altar of the Grandfather.

3.28.m: Nārada said: / Then, O knower of dharma, one should go to the ancient Dharmatīrtha, / where the illustrious Dharma performed supreme ascetic heat.
By him a holy sacred place was made, marked with his own name. / Bathing there, O king, a man devoted to dharma and concentrated,
purifies his family up to the seventh generation; there is no doubt about this. / Then, O knower of dharma, one should go to the excellent Kalāpavanam.
Having gone with great difficulty, and bathing there with concentration, / he obtains the Agniṣṭoma and goes to the realm of Viṣṇu.
Then, O king, a human being should go to the Saugandhika forest, / where the gods headed by Brahmā and the sages rich in ascetic heat,
Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras along with great serpents [dwell]. / Entering that forest, he is immediately freed from all sins.
Then there is the best of rivers, the supreme river of streams, / recorded as the goddess Sarasvatī of the Plakṣa [tree], very holy, O king.
There one should perform ablution in the water issuing from an ant-hill; / having worshipped the ancestors and the gods, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
There is a very rare sacred place named Īśānādhyuṣita. / It is certain that what flows from the ant-hill has sixfold merit at the cascades.
He obtains a thousand brown cows and a horse sacrifice / having bathed there, O tiger among men; this has been seen by the ancients.
Having visited Sugandhā, Śatakumbhā, and Pañcayajña, O Bharata, / the best among men is exalted in the heavenly world.
Having reached the rare sacred place Triśūlapātra right there, / one devoted to worshipping the ancestors and the gods should perform ablution there;
he attains the status of Gaṇeśa's attendant after abandoning the body, without doubt. / Then one should go to Rājagṛha, the very rare place of the Goddess,
celebrated as Śākambharī, renowned in the three worlds. / For a thousand divine years, with greens alone, O Bharata,
she took food month after month, O ruler of men. / Sages rich in ascetic heat, devoted to the Goddess, arrived there,
and hospitality was provided to them with greens alone, O Bharata; / hence her name 'Śākambharī' became established.
Having approached Śākambharī, celibate and concentrated, / having dwelt there for three nights, one should eat greens, self-controlled and pure.
Whatever fruit is properly gained from eating only vegetables for twelve years, / that fruit accrues to him by the wish of the goddess, O descendant of Bharata.
Then one should go to the [place] named Suvarṇa, renowned in the three worlds, / where anciently Kṛṣṇa worshipped Rudra to gain his favor,
and obtained very many boons difficult even for the gods to attain. / And he was told by the slayer of Tripura, who was fully pleased, O Bharata:
'Moreover, you will be dearer to me than myself in the world, O Kṛṣṇa, / and the entire universe will have you as its source; of this there is no doubt.'
Having gone there, O lord of kings, and worshipped the bull-bannered [god], / he obtains the horse sacrifice and attains the status of Gaṇeśa's attendant.
Then a man should go to Dhūmāvatī; having stayed there for three nights, / he obtains the desires requested in his mind; there is no doubt about this.
To the south of the Goddess is Rathāvarta, O ruler of men; / having arrived there, faithful and master of his senses, O knower of dharma,
he goes to the supreme destination through the grace of Mahādeva. / Having turned pradakṣiṇa, one should go, O best of Bharatas,
to the [sacred place] named Dharā, O very wise one, which destroys all sins; / bathing there, O tiger among men, ruler of men, he does not grieve.
Then, O tiger among men, having bowed to the great mountain, one should go / to Gaṅgādvāra, which is undoubtedly equal to the gate of heaven.
There, at Koṭitīrtha, one should perform ablution with concentration; / he indeed obtains [the fruit of] a Puṇḍarīka sacrifice and redeems his family.
Having stayed there for one night, he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows. / At Saptagaṅga, Trigaṅga, and Śakrāvarta, one should offer libations
to the gods and ancestors according to rule; he is exalted in the world of merit. / Then, having bathed at Kanakhala, a man who has fasted for three nights
obtains a horse sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world. / One devoted to sacred places should go to Kapilāvaṭa, O ruler of men;
having stayed there for one night, he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows / at the [abode] of the great-souled serpent-king Kapila, O lord of kings.
the ford famous in all worlds, O best of the Kurus. / There one should perform ablutions at the Nāgatīrtha, O king; / a man attains the fruit of a thousand tawny cows.
Then one should proceed to Lalitikā, the excellent ford of Śaṃtanu. / Having bathed there, O king, a man will not meet a bad rebirth.

3.29.m: Nārada said: / Then one should go, O king of kings, to the excellent ford on the Kālindī. / Having bathed there, O king, a man will not meet a bad rebirth.
Whatever fruit a man obtains at Puṣkara, Kurukṣetra, / Brahmāvarta, Pṛthūdaka, / Avimukta, and Suvarṇākhya,
that fruit he fully attains in the Yamunā, O best of men. / Indeed, for those in whose minds there is a strong desire for heavenly enjoyment,
especially in the Yamunā, by bathing and giving gifts, O best of men, / for those who desire life, health, prosperity, / beauty, youthfulness, and virtues,
the water of the Yamunā should not be abandoned. / Those who fear hell and the like, and those who suffer from poverty in this world,
must by all means diligently perform an immersion there. / For washing away the mud of poverty, sin, and misfortune,

there is indeed nothing else, O Yudhiṣṭhira, except the water of the Yamunā. / Rituals lacking faith are regarded as bearing only half their fruit, / but mere bathing in the Yamunā bestows the full fruit.
Whether free from desire or filled with desire, O king, in the water of the Yamunā, / through immersion he sees no sorrows in this world or the next.
Just as the moon wanes and waxes in the two fortnights, / so sin perishes there and merit increases from bathing.
Just as manifold gems come forth with ease from the ocean, / so life, wealth, wives, and riches arise [from it].
Just as the wish-yielding cow grants one's wish, and the wish-fulfilling jewel gives what is thought of, / even so bathing in the Yamunā grants every desire of the mind.
In the Kṛta age austerity was supreme knowledge; in the Tretā age, sacrifice; / in the Dvāpara and the Kali, giving: but the Kālindī is auspicious at all times.
For all classes and for all stages of life, O ruler of the earth, / immersion in the Yamunā showers dharma in torrential streams.
In this Bhārata land, especially in the realm of action, / the birth of men who do not bathe in the Kālindī is declared fruitless.
Just as there is no majesty in the sky in the lunar orb on the new moon, / so a good deed does not shine without immersion in the Yamunā.
Hari is not so pleased by vows, gifts, and austerities / as Keśava is pleased by mere immersion there.
No radiance is known to equal the radiance of the sun; / in the same way rites born of sacrifices do not equal a bath in the Yamunā.
For the pleasure of Vāsudeva, for the removal of all sins, / and for attaining heaven, a man should immerse himself in the Kālindī.
What is the use of a body preserved, well nourished, and strong, / an impermanent fine body, without bathing in the Yamunā?
It has pillars of bone, bindings of sinews, plaster of flesh and blood, / is bound with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and feces,
pervaded by old age, grief, and calamity, an abode of disease, afflicted, / rooted in passion, non-eternal, and the refuge of all faults,
tormented by the sin of others' welfare, treacherous and envious towards others, / greedy, treacherous, cruel, ungrateful, and transient,
harsh, uncontrollable, wicked, corrupted by the three faults, / impure, burning, foul-smelling, and deluded by the three torments,
by nature delighting in unrighteousness, agitated by hundreds of cravings, / and standing at the gate of hell through desire, anger, and great greed;
bearing the transformed states of worms, feces, and ashes: / such a body is indeed useless without bathing in the Yamunā.
Like bubbles on waters, or unfertilized eggs among birds, / those devoid of bathing in the Yamunā are born merely to die.
A Brahmin who is not a Vaiṣṇava is ruined; a funeral rite without rice-balls is ruined; / a nobility lacking reverence for Brahmins is ruined; a lineage is ruined by bad conduct.
Dharma practiced with hypocrisy is ruined; austerity is ruined by anger; / unsteady knowledge is ruined; sacred learning is ruined through heedlessness.
A woman is ruined by devotion to another; a student of sacred lore is ruined by a woman; / a burnt offering is ruined in an unignited fire; conditional devotion is ruined.
A maiden used as a source of livelihood is ruined; cooking done for oneself is ruined; / yoga practiced while eating food from a Śūdra is ruined; the wealth of a miser is ruined.
Knowledge is ruined by lack of practice; discernment that causes strife is ruined; / a pilgrimage made for livelihood is ruined; a vow undertaken for subsistence is ruined.
Speech is ruined by untruth and likewise by expressing slander; / a mantra heard by six ears is ruined; quiet recitation with an agitated mind is ruined.
A gift given to one unlearned in the Veda is ruined; a people is ruined by disbelief; / everything done for the next world is ruined through lack of faith.
Just as this world is ruined for impoverished men, O king, / so human birth is ruined without immersion in the Kālindī.
All minor sins and great sins / are reduced to ash by immersion in the Yamunā, O king.
All sins tremble when a man approaches the Yamunā: / “What if he should bathe in the water that destroys all sins?”
Best among men shine like fires in the Yamunā, / freed from all sins like the moon released from clouds.
Sin whether wet or dry, light or heavy, committed in speech, mind, or deed— / bathing there consumes it as fire consumes fuel.
Sin committed through heedlessness, and that done knowingly or unknowingly, / is destroyed by mere bathing in the Yamunā, O best of kings.
The sinless go to heaven, and the most sinful attain purity; / no doubt should be entertained here concerning bathing in the water of the Yamunā.
For everyone is eligible here in devotion to Viṣṇu, O king; / goddess Yamunā is always the destroyer of sins for all.
This alone is the supreme mantra, this is the supreme austerity, / and this is the supreme expiation: the excellent bath in the Yamunā.
Men acquire an inclination to bathe in the Kālindī through practice in previous births, / just as skill in spiritual knowledge comes from practice across births, O king.
Skilled at washing away the clinging mud of worldly existence, / the purifying agent of purifiers is the excellent bath in the Yamunā.
Those who have bathed there, O king, in the bestower of the fruit of all desires, / enjoy auspicious pleasures comparable to those of the moon and sun.
The Yamunā is declared to grant liberation if joined with Mathurā; / and at Mathurā, the Kālindī magnifies merit even more abundantly.
Elsewhere the Yamunā is holy and removes grave sins; / joined with Mathurā, the goddess bestows devotion to Viṣṇu.
If accompanied by devotional disposition one immerses in the Kālindī, / one dwells in the presence of Hari for thousands of millions of kalpas.
Men attain liberation indeed without [the need of] Sāṃkhya; / their ancestors are satisfied, remaining content for hundreds of kalpas in heaven.
For those men who drink the auspicious water of the Yamunā, O king, / what need is there of resorting to thousands of the five bovine products?
What need is there of resorting to thousands of millions of fords? / Giving and sacrificial offering made there all become multiplied ten-millionfold.

3.30.m: Nārada said: / On this matter I will narrate to you an ancient legendary history. / Formerly in the Kṛta age, O king, in the excellent city of Niṣadha,
There was a Vaiśya equal to Kubera, named Hemakuṇḍala, / of noble lineage, performing good deeds, who worshipped gods, brāhmaṇas, and fire.
Engaged in agriculture and commerce, buying and selling various wares, / he was devoted to raising cattle, horses, buffaloes, and other animals.
Milk, curd, buttermilk, cow dung, grass, / wood, fruits, roots, salt, ginger, long pepper,
grains, greens, oils, various clothes, / minerals, and sugarcane products, he always sold.
In this way, through diverse means and others as well, O Vaiśya, / he continually acquired eighty million pieces of gold.
Having thus become exceedingly wealthy, his hair turned grey at the ears. / Afterwards, reflecting in his mind on the transience of worldly existence,
he performed righteous deeds with a sixth portion of that wealth: / he built a temple for Viṣṇu and built a house for Śiva.
He caused a vast reservoir, resembling an ocean, to be dug, / and stepwells and ponds of many kinds were built by him.
A forest of banyan, sacred fig, mango, kaṅkola, jambu, neem, and other trees / he then established with his own resources, as well as an auspicious flower garden.
He provided food and drink from sunrise to sunset, / and outside the city, in all four directions, he established beautiful water-booths.
Whatever gifts are famous in the Purāṇas, O king, / that righteous man gave, constantly devoted to giving gifts.
He performed penance for any sin committed throughout his life, / constantly devoted to the worship of the gods, and always honouring guests.
As he lived in this manner, two sons were born to him, O king, / both of renowned names: Śrīkuṇḍala and Vikuṇḍala.
Passing over the household to their charge, he went to the forest for austerity, / and there, worshipping the supreme god Govinda, the boon-giving Lord,
his body emaciated by austerity, his mind ever on Vāsudeva, / he attained the Vaiṣṇava realm, going to which one does not grieve.
Then his two sons, O king, endowed with great pride, / young and handsome, became arrogant with the pride of wealth.
Badly behaved, addicted to vices, neglecting righteous acts and rituals, / they paid no heed to the words of their mother or to the advice of the elders.
Walking bad paths, wicked-minded, spurning their father's friends, / devoted to unrighteousness, malicious, and pursuing other men's wives,
devoted to song and instrumental music, delighting in the lute and the flute, / accompanied by hundreds of courtesans, they wandered about singing.
Surrounded by flatterers, skilled [in seducing women] with bimba-fruit lips, / well-dressed in handsome garments, anointed with lovely sandalwood,
adorned with fragrant garlands, marked with musk, / rich in the beauty of diverse ornaments, wearing delightful pearl necklaces,
sporting here and there with a host of elephants, horses, and chariots, / indulging in drinking liquor, infatuated by passion for other men's wives,
squandering their father's wealth, giving away hundreds and thousands, / they dwelt in their charming house, constantly devoted to pleasures.
Thus that wealth was expended by them on improper expenditures / among courtesans, rakes, actors, wrestlers, bards, and panegyrists.
That wealth was given to unworthy recipients, like seed cast on barren ground; / it was not given to a worthy recipient, nor offered into the mouth of a brāhmaṇa.
Viṣṇu, the supporter of all beings and destroyer of all sins, was not worshipped; / very soon the wealth of both of them came to ruin.
Then they fell into misery and were reduced to extreme penury; / grieving and confounded, they were afflicted by the pain of hunger.
While the two remained in their home, there was nothing to be eaten; / by their own kin, by all their relatives, servants, and dependents,
they were abandoned in the city for lack of wealth, full of worry. / Afterwards, theft was undertaken by the two in the city, O king.
Afraid of the king and of the people, they then departed from their city; / afflicted by all, the two made their dwelling in the forest.
The two fools constantly slaughtered with sharp, poisoned arrows / various birds, boars, and deers and rohita deers,
hares, porcupines, monitor lizards, and many other wild beasts. / Endowed with great strength, associating with Bhillas, they always lived on the spoils of hunting.
Thus eating a diet of meat, consuming sinful food, O scorcher of foes, / once one went to a mountain, and the other went into the forest.
The elder was killed by a tiger, and the younger was bitten by a snake; / on the very same day, O king, the two most sinful men met their death.
Bound by the messengers of Yama, they were led away with their sins to Yama's abode. / Having arrived, all those messengers addressed the two sinners:
“O Dharmarāja, these two men have been brought by your command. / Give the order to your servants: be pleased to tell us what we should do.”
Having deliberated with Citragupta, Yama then spoke to the messengers: / “Let one, O heroes, be led to hell of intense torment;
let the other be placed in heaven, where there are incomparable pleasures.” / Then, hearing the command of the End-maker, by the swift-acting messengers,
he who was the elder, O lord of men, was cast into terrible Raurava. / A certain excellent messenger among them spoke sweet words [to the other]:
“Vikuṇḍala, come with me to heaven; I grant it to you. / Enjoy the most divine pleasures earned by your own action.”

3.31.m: Nārada said: / Then, with a joyful heart, he questioned that messenger on the way, / having harboured a doubt in his heart and filled with supreme wonder, / reflecting in his heart: “For what reason is heaven the fruit for me?”
Vikuṇḍala said: / “O best of messengers, I ask you about a great doubt of mine: / We two were born in the same family, and performed the same deeds.
Our bad death was also the same, and Yama was seen by us alike. / How was my elder brother, who acted identically, cast into hell,
and how did heaven fall to me? Dispel this doubt of mine! / O divine messenger, I do not see the cause of my heaven.”
The divine messenger said: / “Mother, father, son, wife, sister, and brother, O Vikuṇḍala, / these designations are merely the cause of a creature's birth to experience karma.
Just as birds assemble upon a single tree, / so whatever action one desires, influenced by past dispositions, one performs;
and a person always experiences the fruit of that respective action. / Out of affection I tell you the truth: good and bad karma
done by men themselves, O Vaiśya, is experienced from time to time, again and again. / One performs actions alone, and alone enjoys their fruit.
No one is ever tainted by the action of another, O Vaiśya. / Your brother fell into hell due to his very dreadful sins, / and you, O knower of dharma, attain everlasting heaven through dharma.”
Vikuṇḍala said: / “From my childhood my mind was attached to sins, not to merits. / In this birth, O messenger, only wickedness was done by me.
O divine messenger, I do not know of any good deed of my own. / If you know of my merit, please tell it to me out of compassion.”
The divine messenger said: / “Listen, O Vaiśya, I will declare the merit that was accumulated by you; / I know all of it, while you certainly do not know.
There was a brāhmaṇa, the son of Harimitra, named Sumitra, a master of the Vedas; / his holy hermitage was on the southern bank of the Yamunā.
In that forest, friendship arose between you and him, best of vaiśyas; / in his company you bathed for two Māgha months.
In the sacred water of the Yamunā, which takes away all sins and is supreme, / in that sacred site famed across the worlds by the name 'Destroyer of Sin'.
By one [bath] you were freed from all sins, lord of vaiśyas; / by the merit of the second Māgha [bath], you attained heaven, sinless one.
Through the power of that merit, rejoice constantly in heaven! / Your brother suffers great torment of sin in hells;
being cut by sword-leaves and pierced by mallets, / crushed on a slab of rock and roasted in glowing coals.
Hearing the messenger's words, he, distressed by his brother's suffering, / with all his limbs thrilled with horripilation, became wretched and filled with humility.
he spoke sweet, skillful words to that messenger of the gods: / 'Friendship of the good, virtuous one, is formed after seven steps and yields good fruit.
Considering our state of friendship, you ought to assist me. / Therefore I wish to hear, for I consider you omniscient.
By what deed do men not see the world of Yama, / and by what do they go to hell? Tell me that out of compassion.'
The messenger of the gods said: 'You have asked well, vaiśya; your sins are now destroyed. / When a man's heart is purified, his mind turns toward the highest good.
Although I have no free time, being intent on [the god's] service, / nonetheless, out of affection for you, I shall explain according to my understanding.
Those who never, under any circumstances, cause harm to others / in deed, mind, or speech—they do not go to the abode of Yama.
Neither by the Vedas, nor by gifts, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices / do men who harm living beings ever go to heaven.
Non-violence is the highest dharma; non-violence is the supreme austerity; / non-violence is the highest gift—so sages always proclaim.
Those compassionate men who see mosquitoes, reptiles, gadflies, / lice, and men alike, by analogy to themselves—
those men never go to glowing coals, the iron spit, intoxication, the river of spirits, / or the miserable state of the god of death.
Those who harm creatures here, whether living in water or on land, / for the sake of their livelihood, go to the miserable state of Kālasūtra.
There, eating dog meat, drinking pus and blood, / sinking in the mire of fat, they are bitten by downward-facing worms.
Eating one another and striking each other in the darkness, / they dwell for many aeons, uttering a frightful roar of weeping.
Having passed through a hundred births as worms, they become motionless plants for a long time; / then those cruel ones enter hundreds of animal births.
Afterward, those who harmed living beings become born blind, one-eyed, hunchbacked, / lame, impoverished, and missing limbs as human beings.
Therefore, vaiśya, knowing dharma and desiring happiness in both worlds, / one should not perform such acts here or hereafter in deed, mind, or speech.
Those who harm living beings find no happiness in either world; / those who do not harm creatures are not afraid anywhere.
Just as rivers, flowing straight or winding, enter the ocean, / so all dharmas firmly enter into non-violence.
He who has granted fearlessness to creatures here, best of vaiśyas, / has bathed in all sacred sites and has been consecrated in all sacrifices.
Those who observe the duties prescribed in the scriptures, / unmixed with adharma, vaiśya, do not go to the abode of Yama.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the ascetic— / all devoted to their own dharma dwell on the surface of heaven.
All men of the castes and life-stages who conduct themselves as prescribed, / having subdued their senses, go to the eternal world of Brahmā.
Those who are devoted to sacrificial and charitable works, and those devoted to the five great sacrifices, / and who are always endowed with compassion, do not look upon the abode of Yama.
Those capable brahmins who have turned away from sense objects, recite the Veda, / and are constantly engaged in worshipping the sacred fire, go to heaven.
Heroes with undefeated countenances, surrounded by enemies, / who perish in battles—their path is the sun.
Those who give up their lives for the sake of helpless women and brahmins, / and in protecting someone who has sought refuge, vaiśya, do not fall from heaven.
Those who always nourish the lame, the blind, children, the elderly, / the sick, the helpless, and the destitute, vaiśya, always rejoice in heaven.
Men who, seeing a cow sunk in mud or a twice-born sunk in disease, / lift them out, attain the world of those who perform the horse sacrifice.
Those who give a mouthful of grass to cows, who always tend cows, / and who do not mount upon the back of a cow—they dwell in the world of heaven.
Those men who make even a small pit in which a cow's thirst may be quenched, / go to heaven without even seeing the world of Yama.
Those brahmins devoted to worship of the fire, worship of the gods, worship of the guru, / and constantly devoted to worship of the twice-born, go to heaven.
There is no end to the merit of a reservoir, a well, or a pond, / where creatures living in water and on land drink at their own will.
He is said by the wise to be always engaged in giving here; / as often and as much as living beings drink water,
so lasting is the heaven gained through righteous intention, best of vaiśyas. / Water is the life of creatures; vital breaths are grounded in water.
Even men who are sinners are purified by daily bathing; / morning bathing removes external and internal impurities, vaiśya.
Through morning bathing, a man becomes free from sin and does not go to hell; / but he who eats without bathing is always an eater of filth.
The ancestors and deities turn away from the man who does not bathe; / a man lacking a bath is sinful; a man lacking a bath is impure.
One who does not bathe experiences hell and is born among human lice and the like. / But those who perform a bath in a flowing stream on a festival day—
they never go to hell, nor are they born in degraded wombs; / bad dreams and evil thoughts always become barren for them.
For men purified by morning bathing, best of vaiśyas, / who give sesame seeds, vessels of sesame, and a measure of sesame according to rule,
they never go to the realm of the lord of spirits. / Having given land, gold, and a cow, and having offered the sixteen gifts,
they do not turn back from the world of heaven, Vikunḍala! / When a wise person, on auspicious lunar days, at Vyatīpāta, and at a solstice or transit,
having bathed, gives whatever he can, he never sinks into a miserable state. / Givers never tread the terrible path to Raurava, / nor are they born in this world in a family devoid of wealth.
A man who speaks truth, is always silent [when proper], speaks kindly, / is free from anger, has upright conduct, is not excessively talkative, and is not spiteful;
who is always courteous, always compassionate toward creatures, / conceals the vulnerabilities of others, and speaks of others' virtues;
and who does not steal another's property, even a blade of grass, even in his mind— / such people, best of vaiśyas, do not see the torments of hell.
One who slanders others and is a heretic is considered worse than sinners; / he is cooked in hell until the dissolution of all beings.
A speaker of harsh words should be understood as having come from hell; / there is no doubt, best of vaiśyas, that he goes again to a miserable state.
Neither by sacred sites nor by austerities is there an expiation for an ungrateful man; / that man endures terrible torment in hell for a long time.

The person who bathes in whatever sacred waters there are on earth,
with senses conquered and food subdued, does not go to the abode of Yama.

One should not commit a sin at a sacred ford, nor live off a sacred ford;
at a sacred ford, receiving gifts must be abandoned, and selling dharma must be abandoned.

A sin committed at a sacred ford is difficult to digest, and receiving gifts is difficult to digest;
everything at a sacred ford is difficult to digest—how could [one guilty of] this not go to hell?

Bathed but once in the waters of the Gaṅgā, purified by the Gaṅgā's water,
a person does not go to hell, even if he has amassed a heap of sins.

Vows, gifts, austerities, and sacrifices, and other purifying acts,
are not equal to one sprinkled with a drop of the Gaṅgā; so we have heard.

That lowest of men who says the Gaṅgā is equal to other sacred waters
goes, O vaiśya, to a terrible, great hell: Raurava.

For it is liquid dharma, the seed of the waters, fallen from Vaikuṇṭha's foot,
which was held on his head by the Great Lord—that spotless water of the Gaṅgā.

It is truly brahman, no doubt, beyond the qualities, beyond material nature;
with what in the whole cosmic egg could it attain equality?

The person who, even hundreds of leagues away, should say, 'Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā,'
does not go to hell. What could ever be equal to it?
By no other means is an action that leads to hell instantly burned away.

Therefore, humans should make an effort to bathe in the waters of the Gaṅgā.
He who refrains from receiving gifts, even though capable of receiving gifts,
shines, O vaiśya, as a twice-born in the form of a star for a long time in heaven.

Those who rescue a cow from mud, those who protect the sick,
and those who die in a cowpen become stars in the sky.
Those devoted to breath-control do not see the realm of Yama.

Even if they have committed wicked deeds, their sins are destroyed by those alone.
Sixteen breath-controls performed day after day, O vaiśya,
purify daily even the slayer of a brahmin in visible form.

Whatever austerities are practiced, whatever vows and observances are undertaken,
and the giving of a thousand cows—breath-control is equal to that.

A person who drinks a drop of water from the tip of a kuśa blade month after month
for a full hundred years—breath-control is equal to that.

Whatever major sin there is, and likewise minor sins,
a person reduces it all to ashes in an instant by breath-controls.

Those best of men who indeed regard the wives of others like a mother
never, O best of men, go to the tortures of Yama.

He who does not resort to another's wives even in thought,
there is none like him in both worlds; by him, O vaiśya, the earth is upheld.

Therefore, those endowed with dharma should avoid resorting to another's wife;
for another's wives lead [a man] to twenty-one hells.

Those in whose mind longing does not arise for the wives of others
go to the realm of the gods, O best of vaiśyas, not to Yama.

He who is constantly not overcome by anger when occasions for anger arise,
that angerless man on earth should be considered one who has conquered heaven.

The son who worships his mother and father like gods
does not go to the abode of Yama before old age arrives.

And those men who worship their guru with greater esteem than their father
become guests in the world of Brahmā, O best of vaiśyas.

And women here are truly blessed through the preservation of good conduct;
and when good conduct is broken, the realm of Yama is most terrible for women.

Good conduct must always be guarded by women through avoiding wicked company;
for through good conduct the highest heaven is gained by women, O vaiśya, without doubt.

By a cookery-sacrifice and by forbidden conduct practiced by a śūdra,
a miserable state is ordained, O vaiśya; his is an infernal state.

Those who reflect upon the scripture, those devoted to the study of the Veda,
and those who recite and read the Purāṇa and the Saṃhitā,

and those who explain the Smṛtis, who awaken [others] to dharma,
who are seated in the Vedāntas—by them this earth is upheld.

All of them, with their sins destroyed by the greatness of such study,
go to the world of Brahmā, where delusion does not exist.

He who would give the knowledge arising from the Vedas and scriptures to the ignorant,
even those who worship the setting of the Vedas, tears apart the bond of worldly existence.

Hear this wondrous secret, O best of vaiśyas,
approved by Dharmarāja, granting immortality to all the worlds:

The Vaiṣṇavas certainly do not see Yama, nor the realm of Yama,
nor the terrible-looking spirits; truth, truth is spoken by me.

Yamunā's brother always tells us again and again:
'You must avoid the Vaiṣṇavas; they must not fall within my range.

The beings who remember Keśava even once, in passing,
with all the mass of their sins destroyed, go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

A man who worships Viṣṇu, even if he has bad conduct or is an evildoer,
or even if he is devoted to good conduct, must always be avoided by you.

In whose house a Vaiṣṇava eats, and those who have the company of a Vaiṣṇava,
they too should be bypassed by you, their sins destroyed by that company.'

Thus, O vaiśya, the god who holds the staff always commands us;
therefore, the Vaiṣṇavas do not go to the capital of Yama.

Except for devotion to Viṣṇu, there is no other way, O best of vaiśyas,
for most sinful men to cross the ocean of hell.

One should not look at even an outcaste as such, if he is beloved in the world, O vaiśya, and a Vaiṣṇava;
a Vaiṣṇava, even if outside the castes, purifies the three worlds.

The chanting of the Lord's qualities, deeds, and names is sufficient to remove the sins of men,
since even sinful Ajāmila, having cried out to his son 'Nārāyaṇa' while dying, attained liberation.

And the ancestors in both families who have long been submerged in hell
go to heaven at the very moment they worship Hari with joy.

Those who are servants of a devotee of Viṣṇu, and those who eat the food of a Vaiṣṇava,
they, untroubled, go to the state of the sacrifice-eaters [the gods], O vaiśya.

The wise person should solicit the food of a Vaiṣṇava with effort
for the purification of all sins; in its absence, he should drink the water.

If someone dies anywhere murmuring the mantra 'Govinda,'
that man would not see Yama, and we will not look upon him.

Complete with its limbs, with mudrās, with meditation, with its seer, meter, and deity,
he should mutter according to rule, through initiation, the twelve-syllable mantra.

And those best of men who mutter the eight-syllable lord of mantras—
at the sight of them, even a brahmin-slayer is purified, and he shines like Viṣṇu himself.

Bearing conches and discuses, entering within the realm of Brahman,
those men reside in the world of Viṣṇu in the form of Viṣṇu.

Whether in the heart, in the sun, in water, or on an image or sacrificial ground,
having thoroughly worshipped Hari, men go to that abode of Viṣṇu.

Or else Vāsudeva should always be worshipped by seekers of liberation
in a śālagrāma stone, in a gem, or on a discus fashioned by the vajra-insect.

For that is the abode of Viṣṇu, destroying all sins,
bestowing all merits, O vaiśya, and granting liberation to all.

He who worships Hari in the discus originating from a śālagrāma stone,
by him a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices have been performed each day.

The Vedāntas constantly proclaim that Brahman is cessation, the Infallible;
that grace comes to men from the worship of the śālagrāma stone.

Just as fire present in a great log shines forth at the place of sacrifice,
so Hari, the all-pervading, shines forth in a śālagrāma.

Even those of sinful conduct, unqualified for ritual acts,
if they are worshippers of the śālagrāma, O vaiśya, never go to the abode of Yama.
Hari does not delight so much in Lakṣmī, nor does he delight so much in his own abode, / as he always delights in the circle of the Śālagrāma stone.
The agnihotra has been performed by him, and the earth with the oceans has been given away by him, / by whom Hari has been worshipped in the circle born of the Śālagrāma stone.
O vaiśya, if twelve stones born of the Śālagrāma stone / are worshipped according to the rules by anyone, I shall declare his merit to you:
Whatever [merit] there would be through one hundred and twenty million liṅgas worshipped with golden lotuses / across twelve seasons, that is obtained in a single day.
Moreover, he who devotedly worships a hundred Śālagrāma stones / dwells in Hari's realm and is born here as a universal emperor.
Even the lowest of men, when pervaded by lust, anger, and greed, / also goes to Hari's realm through the worship of the Śālagrāma stone.
And the man who joyfully worships Govinda in the Śālagrāma [stone] / does not fall from heaven until the cosmic dissolution.
Without sacred bathing-places, without gifts, without sacrifices, without deep understanding, / men attain liberation, O vaiśya, from worshipping the Śālagrāma stone.
A worshipper of the Śālagrāma stone, even if sinful, O vaiśya, does not go / to hell, or to dwelling in a womb, or to an animal state, or to birth as a worm.
He who knows the rites of initiation and mantras, and offers an oblation upon the circle— / the Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, and Revā, and whichever rivers bestow liberation,
all of them reside indeed in the water of the Śālagrāma stone. / With various food offerings, flowers, incense, lamps, and ointments,
with songs, musical instruments, hymns, and the like, whichever human, / devoted to worship in the Kali age, performs the worship of the Śālagrāma stone,
delights in the presence of Hari for thousands of millions of kalpas. / Whatever fruit is obtained by seeing ten million liṅgas or by worshipping them,
indeed that fruit comes from the Śālagrāma stone in a single day. / When worship is performed even once to the liṅga born of the Śālagrāma stone,
men surely attain liberation, even if devoid of Sāṃkhya knowledge. / Wherever Keśava stands in the form of a Śālagrāma stone,
there are the gods, the suras, the yakṣas, and the fourteen worlds. / But the man who performs a śrāddha on a Śālagrāma stone—
his ancestors remain satisfied in heaven for a hundred kalpas. / Those men who continually drink water from the Śālagrāma stone,
what need have they of partaking of thousands of pañcagavyas? / What need have they of visiting thousands of ten million sacred bathing-places,
if one drinks the holy water that has touched the body of the Śālagrāma stone? / Wherever a Śālagrāma stone is, for three yojanas around is a sacred bathing-place.
There, gifts and fire oblations all become multiplied ten-millionfold. / A man who drinks water from the Śālagrāma stone, even an amount equal to a drop,
never drinks mother's milk again; he partakes of Viṣṇu. / Near a Śālagrāma [stone], indeed for the distance of a krośa all around,
even an insect who dies goes to the supreme abode of Vaikuṇṭha. / He who gives the circle of a Śālagrāma stone as an excellent gift,
by him the entire orb of the earth, along with its mountains and forests, has been given. / The man who sets a price upon a Śālagrāma stone,
and the seller, and he who consents, and he who takes pleasure in its evaluation— / all of them go to hell until the cosmic dissolution.
Therefore, O vaiśya, one should completely avoid the buying and selling of the circle. / What need is there of saying much, O vaiśya? By one who fears sin,
the remembrance of Hari Vāsudeva, which removes all sin, should be performed. / The fruit that a man attains by practicing severe austerity / in the forest with controlled senses,
with senses well restrained, that [very fruit] one obtains by bowing to the Garuḍa-bannered Lord. / Even having committed sin repeatedly, a man overwhelmed by delusion
does not go to hell once he has gone to Hari, who removes all sin. / Whatever sacred bathing-places and holy sanctuaries are upon the earth,
he attains them all from chanting the name of Viṣṇu. / Those dedicated ones who have taken refuge in the god Viṣṇu, holder of the Śārṅga bow,
for them there is no residence in Yama's realm; they would not be dwellers of hell. / A Vaiṣṇava man, O vaiśya, who speaks ill of Śiva
does not find the realm of Viṣṇu; he goes to a great hell. / Having fasted on even a single Ekādaśī, even casually, a man
does not go to Yama's torment; so it has been heard from Lomaśa. / There is nothing so purifying in the three worlds
as either day of the lotus-navelled [Viṣṇu], which destroys wickedness. / Sins reside in this body here, O best of the people,
only so long as a creature does not fast on the auspicious day of the lotus-navelled [Viṣṇu]. / Thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of royal consecration sacrifices
are not worth a sixteenth part of fasting on Ekādaśī. / Whatever sin has been committed through the eleven senses by men, O vaiśya,
By fasting on Ekādaśī, all of that goes to dissolution; / no merit equal to Ekādaśī is found in the world.
Those by whom it is observed even as a pretext do not come under the power of the sun-god's son; / for it bestows heaven and liberation, and grants bodily health.
Indeed, it grants a good wife, and it grants living sons. / Neither the Gaṅgā nor Gayā, O vaiśya, nor Kāśī nor Puṣkara,
nor indeed any Vaiṣṇava sacred field equals the day of Hari; / the Yamunā and the Candrabhāgā do not equal the day of Hari,
by which the Vaiṣṇava abode is attained here without exertion. / Keeping vigil at night and fasting on the day of Hari,
ten ancestors on the paternal side and ten on the maternal side, / and those ten of one's beloved wife, O vaiśya—he undoubtedly delivers them.
Free from the attachment to dualities, having made their dwellings no longer domestic, / wearing garlands and clad in yellow garments, they go to the abode of Hari.
In childhood, or in youth, or in old age, O best of the vaiśyas, / having fasted on Ekādaśī, certainly even a sinner does not go to extreme misfortune.
Fasting for three nights here, or bathing at sacred places, / and giving gold, sesame seeds, and cows, men go to heaven in this world.
Those who do not bathe at sacred places, O vaiśya, and by whom no gold has been given, / and by whom no austerity has been performed at all—they will be sorrowful everywhere.
Briefly spoken is dharma and the description of hell: / harmlessness toward all beings through speech, mind, and bodily actions;
restraint of the senses, generosity, worship of Hari, / and always observing the duties of caste and life-stage according to the rules.
One who desires heaven should never proclaim his austerity or gift, O vaiśya; / he should give according to his capacity, desiring the welfare of himself.
Footwear, cloth, foods, leaves, roots, fruits, and water: / a day should not be made fruitless, even by a poor man, O vaiśya.
What is not given does not serve one in this world or in the next; / givers do not see those various torments of Yama.
They become long-lived and rich in wealth here again and again. / What is the use of speaking much on this? By adharma they go to an evil state;
by dharma men ascend to heaven everywhere and at all times.
Therefore, starting from childhood, the accumulation of dharma should be made. / Thus everything has been told to you; what else do you wish to hear?
Vikuṇḍala said: / Having heard your words, gentle one, my mind has indeed become serene. / Gaṅgā water destroys sin at once; the word of the good removes sin.
To do good and to speak kindly is the innate quality of the virtuous; / by whom is the cool-rayed moon made into a cool orb of nectar?
O divine messenger, therefore tell me who am asking out of compassion: / How may immediate deliverance from hell arise for my brother?
Hearing his words, the divine messenger spoke, / observing his meditation, contemplating for a moment, bound by the cord of his friendship.
'Whatever merit was accumulated by you in your eighth birth, O vaiśya, / let all of that be given to your brother, if you desire heaven for him.'
Vikuṇḍala said: / 'What is that merit, how did it arise, and what was that former birth? / Let all that be told, messenger; then I will give it immediately.'
The divine messenger said: / 'Listen, O vaiśya, I will tell you of that merit together with its cause. / Formerly, in the holy Madhuvana, there was a sage named Śākuni,
endowed with austerity and sacred study, equal to Brahmā in splendors. / To him through Revatī were born nine sons, like planets:
Dhruva, Śīla, Budha, Tāra, and Jyotiṣmat the fifth; / these were devoted to the agnihotra fire and delighted in the duties of a householder.
Nirmoha, Jitakāma, Dhyānakośa, and Guṇādhika: / these four sons of the twice-born were detached from householder life.
Having entered the fourth stage of life, free from all desires, / staying for one night in a village, without attachments, without possessions,
without cravings, effortless, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal, / covered with whatever was at hand, fed on whatever was at hand,
gathering food only in the evening, and constantly devoted to meditation on Viṣṇu, / conquerors of sleep, conquerors of food, enduring wind and cold,
seeing the entire world, moving and unmoving, in the form of Viṣṇu, / they wandered about freely on the earth, established in mutual silence.
Those yogins performed no ritual acts, being dedicated solely to the highest reality, / having perceived knowledge, without doubts, skilled in the transformations of consciousness.
Thus, when you were a brāhmaṇa in your eighth prior birth, / living in the Middle Country, endowed with sons, wife, and household,
they came to your house at midday, hungry and thirsty, / at the time following the vaiśvadeva rite; and they were seen by you in the courtyard of your home.
With a faltering voice, with tearful eyes, with joy, and with agitation, / prostrating like a staff, preceded by great respect,
bowing with your head to their feet and making an añjali with both hands, / they were all welcomed by you then with sincere and pleasant words:
“Today my birth has become fruitful, and my life is fruitful as well; / today Viṣṇu is pleased with me, today I have a protector and am purified;
today I am blessed, my house is blessed, and my family members are blessed today; / today my ancestors are blessed, and blessed are the cows, sacred learning, and wealth;
since your feet, which remove the three kinds of suffering, were seen by me. / Because the sight of you is like the sight of Hari himself for a blessed person.”
Having thus worshiped them and washed their feet, / it was placed on your head, O best of the vaiśyas, with supreme faith then.
Where the foot-water was placed on your head with faith, O vaiśya, / and having worshiped them with fragrances, flowers, unbroken grains, incenses, and lamps with devotion,
the ascetics were thus fed with delicious food; / satisfied, those paramahaṃsas rested in your house during the night,
meditating upon the supreme Brahman, which is considered the light of lights. / The merit born of hospitality toward them that arose for you, O best of vaiśyas—
indeed, I cannot declare that even with a thousand mouths. / Living creatures are the highest among beings; among living creatures, those living by intellect;
among the intelligent, gods are best; among men, the brāhmaṇa classes; / among brāhmaṇas, the learned; and among the learned, those of resolved intellect;

among those of resolved intellect, the performers of duty; and among performers of duty, the knowers of Brahman. / Therefore they are truly worthy of worship, and thus the highest in the three worlds.
Association with them, O best of vaiśyas, destroys great sins. / Satisfied, the knowers of Brahman resting in a householder's home
destroy in an instant sin accumulated since birth. / Whatever sin of a householder has been accumulated until the end of life,
an ascetic who has stayed for one night completely burns it all. / Give that merit to your brother, by which he will be freed from hell.'
Hearing the messenger's words, the brother quickly gave his religious merit / with a joyful heart, and he too departed from hell.
Honored by the gods with a shower of flowers, they both went to heaven. / Thoroughly worshiped by the two, the messenger departed as he had come.

Having heard the words of the divine messenger, which bring awakening to the entire world and are equal to Vedic statements, / and having saved his brother by the gift of his own accumulated merit, the son of the vaiśya went with him to the supreme realm of Indra.
Whoever, O king, recites or even listens to this legendary history, / freed from sorrow, attains the fruit of the gift of a thousand cows.

3.32.m: Nārada said: / Then one should go, O king of kings, to the world-renowned Sugandha; / purified of all sins, one is honoured in the realm of Brahmā.
Then, O ruler of men, the pilgrim visiting sacred bathing-places should go to Rudrāvarta; / having bathed there, O king, a man is honoured in the heavenly realm.
And at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī, O best of men, / having bathed, one obtains [the merit of] a horse sacrifice and goes to the heavenly realm.
Having bathed there in Karṇahrada and worshipped god Śaṅkara, / one does not meet an unfortunate state and goes to the heavenly realm.
Then the pilgrim visiting sacred bathing-places should go in order to Kubjāmraka; / he obtains [the merit of giving] a thousand cows and goes to the heavenly realm.
The pilgrim visiting sacred bathing-places should go to Arundhatīvaṭa, O ruler of men; / having touched the water at Sāmudraka and fasted for three nights, a man
would obtain the fruit of a thousand cows and goes to the heavenly realm. / Then one should go to Brahmāvarta, celibate and concentrated;
he obtains [the merit of] a horse sacrifice and goes to the heavenly realm. / One should go to the source of the Yamunā; having touched the water of the Yamunā,
and having obtained the fruit of a horse sacrifice, he is honoured in the realm of Brahmā. / Having reached Darvīsaṃkramaṇa, the sacred bathing-place famed across the three worlds,
he obtains [the merit of] a horse sacrifice and goes to the heavenly realm. / And having gone to the source of the Sindhu, frequented by siddhas and gandharvas,
having dwelt there for five nights, he should give away much gold. / Then, reaching the Goddess who is exceedingly difficult to access,
a man obtains [the merit of] a horse sacrifice and would go to the realm of Uśanas. / Having reached Ṛṣikulyā and Vasiṣṭha, O Bhārata—
having passed beyond Vasiṣṭha, all the castes and the twice-born— / a man, having bathed in Ṛṣikulyā, proceeds to the realm of the ṛṣis.
If he should reside there for a month subsisting on vegetables, O ruler of men, / and reaching Bhṛgutuṅga, he would obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
And having gone to Vīrapramokṣa, he is freed from all sins. / And having reached the rare sacred bathing-place of Kārtika and Māgha,
the meritorious doer obtains the fruit of both the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices. / Then, having reached Saṃdhyā, the unsurpassed Vidyātīrtha,
if he touches its water, he will reach the further shore of all knowledges. / He should reside for a night in Mahāśrama, which frees one from all sins;
taking no food for one mealtime, he dwells in auspicious worlds. / Residing for a month at Mahālaya with fasting at the sixth mealtime,
having crossed over, he causes ten ancestors and ten descendants to cross over. / Having seen the holy, supreme Māheśvara honoured by the gods,
having accomplished his purpose in all duties, he never grieves over death; / purified of all sins, he would acquire much gold.

Then one should go to Vetasikā, frequented by the Grandfather;
he attains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice and reaches the supreme state.

Then reaching the sacred ford Sundarikā, frequented by Siddhas,
he becomes an enjoyer of beauty; this was seen by the ancients.

Then going to Brāhmaṇikā, celibate and composed,
he reaches the world of Brahmā in a chariot of lotus hue.

And then one should go to Naimiṣa, holy and frequented by Brahmins;
there Brahmā dwells perpetually along with the hosts of gods.

Half of the sin of one longing for Naimiṣa is destroyed;
and the man who has merely entered is freed from all sin.

A wise man, devoted to sacred fords, should dwell there in Naimiṣa for a month;
whatever sacred fords there are on earth are there in Naimiṣa, O descendant of Bharata.

Having performed ablution there, restrained and eating measured food,
a human being attains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.

He purifies his family up to the seventh generation, O best of Bharatas,
who, devoted to fasting, abandons his life breaths at Naimiṣa.

He rejoices dwelling in the heavenly world—thus the wise have said;
Naimiṣa is perpetually pure and holy, O best of kings.

Having reached Gaṅgodbheda, a man having fasted for three nights
attains [the fruit of] a Vājapeya and becomes perpetually absorbed in Brahman.

Having reached the Sarasvatī, one should offer libations to the ancestors and gods;
he rejoices in the worlds of Sarasvatī, there is no doubt about this.

And then one who frequents sacred fords should go to Bāhudā, O ruler of men;
having stayed there for one night, he is glorified in the heavenly world.

A human being attains the fruit of the divine sacrificial session;
and then one should go to Rajanī, holy and attended by holy folk.

Devoted to worshiping ancestors and gods, he would attain [the fruit of] a Vājapeya;
having reached Vimalāśoka, he shines like the moon.

Having stayed there for one night, he is glorified in the heavenly world;
then one should go to Gopratāra, an excellent sacred ford on the Sarayū,

where Rāma went to heaven together with servants, army, and mounts,
having abandoned his home in the past, O king, through the power of that sacred ford,

and by Rāma's grace and his own resolve, O descendant of Bharata;
having bathed in that sacred ford Gopratāra, O ruler of men,

his soul purified of all sin, he is glorified in the heavenly world;
having bathed at Rāmatīrtha on the Gomatī, O delight of the Kurus,

a man attains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice and purifies his family;
there is the sacred ford Śatasāhasraka there, O best of Bharatas.

Having touched the water there, restrained and eating measured food,
he attains the holy fruit of a thousand cows, O bull of Bharatas.

Then one should go, O knower of dharma, to the unsurpassable Ūrdhvasthāna;
having bathed at Koṭitīrtha, O king, and having worshiped Guha,

he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows and also becomes radiant;
then going to Vārāṇasī and worshiping the bull-bannered [Śiva],

and having bathed in the pool of the Kapilās, he obtains the fruit of a Rājasūya;
having reached the rare sacred ford of Mārkaṇḍeya, O lord of kings,

at the world-famous confluence of the Gomatī and the Gaṅgā,
he attains [the fruit of] an Agniṣṭoma and thoroughly elevates his family.

3.33.m:
Nārada said:
In this regard I shall relate the legendary history concerning the virtues of Vārāṇasī,
by the mere hearing of which one is freed from the murder of a Brahmin.

Formerly on the peak of Meru, the Goddess seated on a divine seat
asked the god, the Sovereign, the enemy of Tripura, Mahādeva:

The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, destroyer of the distress of devotees,
how does a person behold you, the god, in no time at all?

Sāṃkhya-yoga, likewise meditation, karma-yoga, or Vedic practice,
and whatever other practices there are in the world, O Śaṅkara, involve great exertion;

by what [means] is the Lord, subtle, to be seen indeed
by yogins, by workers whose minds are resting, and by all embodied beings?

Tell this most secret knowledge, hidden, attended to by Indra and the gods,
for the benefit of all beings, which destroys the fire of desire.

My supreme and most secret sacred field is the city of Vārāṇasī,
which carries all beings indeed across the ocean of worldly existence.

There, through devotion, O great goddess, undertaking my vow,
great souls dwell, adhering to the supreme discipline.

The best of all sacred fords, and the best of all abodes,
the best knowledge among types of knowledge is my supreme Avimukta.

Holy sacred fords and temples are in other locations,
fixed on cremation grounds, and located in celestial lands;

my abode is in the atmosphere, not touching the earthly realm at all;
the unliberated see it there, while the liberated see it with the mind.

This cremation ground is famous, renowned as Avimukta;
becoming Time, I dissolve this world here, O beautiful one.

O goddess, this place is the dearest to me among all secrets;
my devotees go there and enter into me alone.

Whatever is given, muttered, offered into fire, sacrificed, whatever austerity is performed,
meditation, study, and knowledge—everything becomes imperishable there.

Whatever sin has been accumulated previously in thousands of other births,
all of that goes to destruction for one who has entered Avimukta.

Brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, śūdras, and mixtures of castes,
women, mlecchas, and whatever other mixed beings of sinful wombs,

insects and ants, and whatever other beasts and birds,
reaching their demise in due course in Avimukta, O fair-faced one,

with crests of crescent moons, three-eyed, riding great bulls,
men are born there in my auspicious city, O goddess.

No sinner having died in Avimukta goes to hell;
for, graced by the Lord, all go to the supreme state.

Considering liberation very difficult to attain and worldly existence exceedingly terrible,
a man should break both feet with a stone and dwell in Vārāṇasī.

Rare even through austerity is that state which frees one from worldly existence,
for one who has died, O supreme sovereign, having perished anywhere [there].

It arises properly by my grace, O daughter of the king of mountains;
the unevolved do not see it, deluded by my māyā.

They dwell again and again in the midst of feces, urine, and semen;
yet that wise man who would dwell there, even though stricken by hundreds of obstacles,

he goes to the supreme abode, having gone where he does not grieve;
they go to the supreme abode of Śiva, freed from birth, death, and old age.

That indeed is the state of those who do not die again, of those who desire liberation,
having reached which one would be one who has accomplished his purpose—thus the learned consider.

Not by gifts, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices, nor even by learning
is that eminent state attained which is obtained in Avimukta.

People of various castes and outcasts, cāṇḍālas and other contemptible ones,
and those whose bodies are filled with offenses and severe sins,

the wise know Avimukta to be the supreme medicine for them;
Avimukta is supreme knowledge, Avimukta is the supreme abode;

Avimukta is the supreme truth, Avimukta is supreme Śiva;
having undergone a lifelong initiation, those who dwell in Avimukta—
I give them that supreme knowledge, and in the end the highest state. / Prayāga, Naimiṣa Forest, Śrīśaila, and Mahābala,
Kedāra, Bhadrakarṇa, Gayā, and Puṣkara, / Kurukṣetra, Bhadrakoṭi, the Narmadā, and Āmrātakeśvarī,
Śālagrāma, Kubjāmra, unsurpassable Kokāmukha, / Prabhāsa, Vijayeśāna, Gokarṇa, and Bhadrakarṇaka—
these sacred places are renowned in the three worlds, / yet they do not reach the supreme reality as do those who have died in Vārāṇasī.
Especially in Vārāṇasī, the Ganges flowing along three paths, / when entered, destroys sin committed over hundreds of other lifetimes.
Elsewhere the Ganges, ancestral rites, giving, asceticism, recitation of mantras, / and vows are easy to find; all of this is very difficult to find in Vārāṇasī.
A man living in Vārāṇasī who constantly recites, offers oblations, / gives, worships the immortals, and continually feeds on air—
whether he is a sinner, whether he is a scoundrel, or whether he is a righteous man, / by reaching Vārāṇasī, he purifies his entire family.
Those who worship and praise Mahādeva in Vārāṇasī, / freed from all sins, are to be understood as lords of the Gaṇas.
Elsewhere, through yoga and knowledge, or through renunciation elsewhere, / that supreme abode is reached only after a thousand lifetimes.
Those devotees, O ruler of the gods, who dwell in Vārāṇasī, / attain supreme liberation in just a single lifetime.
Where yoga, knowledge, and liberation [come] in a single birth, / having reached that Avimukta, one should desire no other penance grove.
Because it was never abandoned by me, it is remembered as Avimukta. / It is the secret of secrets; this is called discernment.
For those devoted to knowledge and non-knowledge who desire supreme bliss, / whatever state is known, O fair-browed one, that belongs to one who dies in Avimukta.
Whatever [spots] of Avimukta are seen completely in the body, / the city of Vārāṇasī is even superior and more auspicious than those places.
Where, directly at the end of the body, the Lord Mahādeva himself / explains the saving Brahman right there for the sake of liberation;
That which is heard as the higher reality called Avimukta, / one may attain that in a single lifetime in Vārāṇasī, O goddess.
Between the brows, in the navel, in the heart, and likewise at the crown of the head, / just as Avimukta is situated in the sun, so it is in Vārāṇasī.
And within this, between the Varaṇā [and the Asī], is the city of Vārāṇasī; / right there the reality is established, always thus detached.
There was never a higher place than Vārāṇasī, nor will there ever be, / where the god Nārāyaṇa, Mahādeva, and the Lord in heaven dwell;
Where the gods together with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, serpents, and Rākṣasas / constantly revere him, as does the god of gods, the Grandfather [Brahmā].
O goddess, great sinners, even those who have committed the worst sins, / by reaching Vārāṇasī, attain the supreme state.
Therefore, a seeker of liberation, restrained, should dwell [there] until death. / Obtaining knowledge from Mahādeva in Vārāṇasī, he is liberated.
However, obstacles will arise for one whose mind is afflicted by sin; / therefore one should not commit sin with body, mind, or speech.
This is the secret of the gods and the Purāṇas, O lady of good vows; / no one truly understands the knowledge that rests on Avimukta."
Nārada said: / "While the gods and the supreme ṛṣis were listening, / this destroyer of all sins was spoken by the god of gods:
Just as Nārāyaṇa is the best of the gods, the Supreme Spirit, / and as Giriśa is the best of lords, so is this the best of places.
Those by whom Rudra was propitiated in a previous lifetime / know this supreme field, Avimukta, the abode of Śiva.
Those whose minds are impaired, having arisen from the impurities of Kali, / are not able to know that abode of the Supreme Lord.
Those who always remember and speak of this city, / their sin is quickly destroyed here and in the hereafter.
And whatever sins those who have made their dwelling here commit, / the god Śiva, whose body is Time, destroys all of them.
One should come to this place resorted to by those who desire liberation, / and for those who die [here], there is no rebirth in the ocean of worldly existence.
Therefore, with every effort, a man should dwell in Vārāṇasī, / whether a yogi or a non-yogi, a sinner or a performer of most virtuous deeds.
Not by the words of people, nor of parents, nor by the speech of a guru, / should the mind be diverted from proceeding toward Avimukta."

3.34.m: Nārada said: / "There is this pure, auspicious liṅga named Oṃkāra, / merely by the remembrance of which one is freed from all sins.
This higher knowledge, the excellent group of five shrines, / is constantly resorted to by sages in Vārāṇasī, bestowing liberation.
There Mahādeva himself, in the form of the five shrines, / the blessed Lord Rudra who grants release to living beings, takes delight.
This Pāśupata knowledge is called the five shrines; / it is this pure liṅga, Oṃkāra, that is present.
Beyond Peace, Peace, Higher and Lower Knowledge, / Support, and Withdrawal—such is the fivefold divine liṅga.
The support even of the five liṅgas, Brahmā and the others, / the liṅga that makes known [Oṃ]kāra is called the five shrines.
A wise man who remembers the imperishable divine liṅga of the five shrines, / enters the supreme light and bliss at the end of the body.
There in former times, divine sages, perfected ones, and brahmin sages, / having worshipped the Lord Īśāna, attained the supreme state in the end.
On the holy bank of the Matsyodarī is the most secret, auspicious place, / measuring merely a bull's hide, O king of kings: the excellent [Oṃ]kāreśvara,
the Kṛttivāseśvara liṅga, the excellent Madhyameśvara, / Viśveśvara, likewise Oṃkāra, and Kandarpeśvara.
These are the secret liṅgas in Vārāṇasī, O Yudhiṣṭhira; / no one knows them here without the grace of Śambhu.
Listen, O king, to the glorification of Kṛttivāseśvara: / at that place in ancient times a daitya became an elephant and [came] into Śiva's presence,
arriving to kill the brahmins where they constantly worshipped; / from their liṅga Mahādeva, the three-eyed one, appeared.
For the sake of protecting his devotees, Mahādeva, who is affectionate to his devotees, / Hara, having disdainfully slain with his trident the daitya in the form of an elephant,
made its hide his clothing, and hence he is Kṛttivāseśvara. / There, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the sages attained supreme perfection,
and in that very body they attained that supreme state. / The Rudras who are the Vidyāvidyeśvaras and those proclaimed to belong to Śiva,
continually dwell relying upon the Kṛttivāseśvara liṅga. / Knowing the Kali yuga to be terrible and full of unrighteousness, people
do not leave Kṛttivāsa; by that they have accomplished their aim, without a doubt. / Liberation, which may or may not be attained elsewhere after a thousand lifetimes,
liberation is attained in a single lifetime here at Kṛttivāsa. / Indeed, they call this place the dwelling of all perfected beings,
concealed by the god of gods, Mahādeva Śambhu. / Here, in age after age, self-controlled brahmins who have mastered the Vedas [dwell].

They worship the Great Soul and chant the Śatarudrīya hymn; / they constantly praise the god, the three-eyed one clad in hides; / they meditate in their hearts upon the god, the immovable, inward Śiva of all.
Indeed, the Siddhas sing songs: "For the brāhmaṇas who dwell in Vārāṇasī, / who have taken refuge with the one clad in hides, liberation comes in a single birth."

Having obtained in the world a birth in brāhmaṇa lineages—desired by all worlds and exceedingly hard to attain— / having concentrated in meditation, ascetics chant Rudra and meditate in their hearts upon the Great Lord.
Residing in the midst of Vārāṇasī, the great sages worship the Lord, the Ruler; / free from selfish motives, they sacrifice with offerings, praise Rudra, and bow to Śambhu:

"Salutation to Bhava, the abode of stainless yoga! I take refuge in the immovable one, the ancient Lord of the Mountain! / I remember Rudra seated in the heart; I know the Great God who has manifold forms."

3.35.m: Nārada said: / Now, there is another excellent liṅga there named Kapardīśvara. / Having bathed there according to rule and satiated the ancestors, O king,
