one is freed from all sins and attains enjoyment and liberation. / Beyond that is located another sacred bath named Piśācamocana.
There the wondrous god grants liberation and removes all faults. / Once a certain Daitya, a tiger bearing a terrifying form, went there
to the excellent Kapardīśvara in order to devour a doe. / There, her heart terrified, she circumambulated again and again,
and as she ran completely bewildered, she fell into the power of the tiger. / Tearing her apart with his sharp claws, that exceedingly powerful tiger
went away to another deserted region upon seeing the great sages. / As soon as she died in front of Kapardīśa, that young doe
was seen as a great flame in the sky, radiant as the sun, / three-eyed, blue-throated, with hair marked by the crescent moon,
mounted upon a bull and surrounded by attendants resembling herself. / From all around, sky-dwellers showered rains of flowers upon her.
Having become a female leader of the Gaṇas herself, she was seen no more from that moment. / Seeing that supreme wonder, the gods and others offered praise.
That excellent liṅga of the Great Lord is Kapardīśvara; / merely by remembering it, one is quickly freed from an entire flood of sins.
The faults such as desire and anger belonging to the inhabitants of Vārāṇasī, / and all obstacles, are destroyed through the worship of Kapardīśvara.
Therefore, the excellent Kapardīśvara should always be seen, / carefully worshipped, and praised with Vedic hymns.
And for yogins of peaceful mind who meditate constantly here, / the perfection of yoga arises in six months; there is no doubt.
Sins such as killing a brāhmaṇa are destroyed through its worship, / since one who has bathed in the Piśācamocana pool attains peace.
In that sacred place long ago, an ascetic brāhmaṇa of strict vows / renowned as Śaṅkukarṇa worshipped Śaṅkara.
He constantly chanted Rudra and the Praṇava, which is identical to Brahman, / with flowers, incense, and the like, with hymns, salutations, and circumambulations.
Engrossed in yoga, having undertaken a life-long vow, he worshipped there. / Once, he saw a ghost arrive, stricken with hunger,
its limbs bound only by bone and skin, sighing again and again. / Seeing him, that best of sages, filled with supreme compassion,
said: "Who are you? From what country have you resorted to this country?" / Afflicted by hunger, the Piśāca spoke these words to him:
"In my previous birth, I was a brāhmaṇa endowed with wealth and grain, / accompanied by sons, grandsons, and others, eager to maintain my family.
The Great God was not worshipped by me, nor cows, nor guests, / nor was merit ever performed, whether small or great.
Once, the divine Lord whose mount is the lord of bulls, / Viśveśvara, was seen, touched, and saluted by me in Vārāṇasī.
Then, after a long time, I attained death. / That exceedingly terrible abode of Yama was not seen by me, O sage.
Now overpowered by thirst, I do not know what is beneficial or harmful. / If, O lord, you see any means to deliver me,
please employ it! Salutations to you; I have come to you for refuge!" / Addressed thus, Śaṅkukarṇa then spoke this to the Piśāca:
"Indeed, no doer of merit greater than you exists in this world, / since the divine Viśveśvara, Śiva, was formerly seen by you,
touched, and praised again! Who else is equal to you on earth? / Due to the ripening of that karma, you have arrived in this region.
Quickly take a bath with concentrated mind in this pool, / by which you will immediately abandon this vile state of birth."
Addressed thus by the compassionate sage, the Piśāca, remembering the three-eyed foremost of gods, / Kapardīśvara, the Ruler, focused his mind and plunged into the water.

Having bathed there in the presence of the sage, he died and became endowed with divine ornaments; / he was seen in an aerial chariot, resembling the sun, his lovely crown marked by the crescent moon.
He shone accompanied by Rudras dwelling in heaven, surrounded by immeasurable, foremost yogins / and the Vālakhilyas and others—this god, like the sun, the lord of all gods, at its rising.
In heaven, the hosts of Siddhas and gods praise him, and delightful celestial Apsarases dance; / Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, and others shower rains of flowers mixed with water.
Being praised then by hosts of great sages, having attained knowledge by the grace of the Lord, / he entered that supreme sphere consisting of the three Vedas, where Rudra shines.
Seeing that the Piśāca had become liberated, the sage, delighted in mind, / contemplating the Great Lord, Rudra, the wise one, the unique fire, bowed and praised that Kapardin:
Śaṅkukarṇa said: / "I go to you, Kapardin, who are beyond the beyond, the sole protector, the ancient Puruṣa, / the Lord of Yoga, the object of desire, the sun, the fire, who ride the tawny cow.

To you, the essence of Brahman seated in the heart, the golden yogin who are the beginning and the end, / I go for refuge—to Rudra who dwells in heaven, the great sage, consisting of Brahman, the pure one.
Possessing a thousand feet, eyes, and heads, of a thousand forms, beyond darkness— / to that Śambhu, the supreme boundary of Brahman, the lord of Hiraṇyagarbha, the three-eyed one, I bow.
In whom is the origin and the destruction of the universe, by whom as Śiva all this is pervaded— / to that Lord, the Ruler, the supreme boundary of Brahman, having bowed, I constantly take refuge.

Devoid of mark, of form beyond perception, the self-luminous master, the lord of consciousness, uniform— / to you, the supreme Lord, the supreme boundary of Brahman, I shall pay homage, than whom there is nothing else.

Whom yogins who have abandoned seeded yoga, having attained absorption and become the Supreme Self, / behold—to that god, whose essential nature is supreme, the supreme boundary of Brahman, I am perpetually bowed.

In whom there is no conceptualisation of distinct features such as name, whose essential form does not stand within sight— / to you, the self-existent one, the supreme boundary of Brahman, I am perpetually bowed and take refuge.

Whom those devoted to the teachings of the Veda behold as bodiless, identical with the knowledge of Brahman, one without difference, / yet manifold as your own form—to that supreme boundary of Brahman, I am perpetually bowed."
From whom the primordial matter [originates], the ancient spirit bears his splendor, and the gods bow down— / I bow to him who is situated in the light, the great Time, your true nature.
I constantly take refuge in the Lord of the cave; I take refuge in Sthāṇu, the ancient Giriśa; / I take refuge in Śiva, Hari, the moon-crested one, bearer of the Pināka; I go to you for refuge.
Having thus praised the Lord Kapardin, / Śaṅkukarṇa fell like a staff upon the ground, loudly uttering the supreme praṇava.
At that moment a supreme linga appeared, consisting of Śiva, / infinite knowledge and bliss, resembling the fiery flame of ten million fires.
Then the liberated-souled Śaṅkukarṇa, having become identical with it, all-pervading and stainless, / dissolved into that pure linga; it was as though a wondrous marvel occurred.
This secret has been told to you, the glorification of Kapardin; / no one knows it because of darkness; even a learned person is bewildered in this matter.
Whoever hears this sin-destroying story constantly, / cleansed of all sins, purified in soul, attains closeness to Rudra.
And whoever, purified, constantly recites the great praise, the Brahmapāra, / at dawn and at midday, will attain the supreme yoga.

3.36.m: Nārada said: / In Vārāṇasī, O great king, is Madhyameśa, higher than the highest. / In that place, Mahādeva, the great lord, along with the goddess,
the Lord delights constantly, surrounded by the Rudras. / Formerly, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Soul of all, the son of Devakī,
Kṛṣṇa dwelt there for a year, always accompanied by Pāśupatas, / his entire body smeared with ashes, devoted to the study of the Rudra hymns,
worshipping Śambhu, Hari having undertaken the Pāśupata vow. / His many disciples, devoted to celibacy,
having obtained knowledge from his mouth, beheld the great lord. / The god Mahādeva, Nīlalohita, visibly appeared to him;
the boon-giving Lord granted an excellent boon to Kṛṣṇa: / 'Whoever worships Govinda, being devoted to me according to the prescribed rules,
to them that divine knowledge comprising the world shall arise. / He is to be paid homage, worshipped, and meditated upon by people devoted to me.
Twice-born ones will arise by my grace, without doubt. / Those who see the Lord of gods here, the god wielding the Pināka, having bathed,
their sins, such as slaying a brahmin, are immediately destroyed. / Mortals who relinquish their vital breaths here, even if attached to sinful deeds,
they go to that supreme abode; no doubt should be entertained here. / Truly fortunate are those wise ones who have offered water in the Mandākinī,
having worshipped Mahādeva, the Lord Madhyameśvara. / Knowledge, charity, austerity, śrāddha, and the offering of rice balls here,
each deed performed purifies up to seven generations of the family. / By bathing at Sannihatī when the sun is seized by Rāhu,

whatever fruit a mortal obtains, ten times that is obtained here. / Thus, O great king, the glorification of Madhyameśvara has been told; / whoever hears it with supreme devotion goes to the supreme abode.

3.37.m: Nārada said: / And hear now, O great king Yudhiṣṭhira, / of other purifying holy places situated here in Vārāṇasī.
There is a holy place greater than Prayāga, the supremely auspicious Prayāga, / and likewise the holy place Viśvarūpa, and the unsurpassed Tālatīrtha;
the great holy place called Ākāśa, and the supreme Ārṣabha holy place; / the great holy place Sunīla, and the unsurpassed Gaurītīrtha;
likewise the Prājāpatya holy place, and also Svargadvāra; / that which is called Jambukeśvara, and the excellent holy place named Dharma;
the supreme Gayā holy place, and likewise the holy place Mahānadī; / the supreme Nārāyaṇa holy place, and the unsurpassed Vāyutīrtha;
the supreme secret Jñānatīrtha, and the excellent Vārāhatīrtha; / the meritorious Yamatīrtha, and the auspicious Sammūrtika holy place;
Agnitīrtha, O great king, and the excellent Kalaśeśvara; / Nāgatīrtha, Somatīrtha, and likewise Sūryatīrtha;
the great secret called Parvata, and the unsurpassed Maṇikarṇya; / the excellent holy place Ghaṭotkaca, Śrītīrtha, and Pitāmaha;
and the Gaṅgātīrtha of the Lord of the gods, the excellent holy place of Yayāti; / Kāpila, Someśa, and the unsurpassed Brahmatīrtha.
When Brahmā arrived there to install the ancient linga, / at that time Viṣṇu installed that linga of the Lord.
Having bathed there and approached, Brahmā said to Hari: / 'This linga was brought by me; why have you installed it?'
Viṣṇu said to him: 'Even more than yours, my devotion to Rudra is firm. / Therefore, the linga installed will be named after you.'
And likewise the holy place Bhūteśvara, and the holy place originated from Dharma; / the very auspicious Gandharvatīrtha, and the excellent Vāhneyatīrtha;
Daurvāsika, Vyomatīrtha, and Candratīrtha, O Yudhiṣṭhira; / the holy place Cintāṅgadeśvara, and the sacred Vidyādhareśvara;
the Kedāratīrtha named Ugra, and the unsurpassed Kālañjara; / Sārasvata, Prabhāsa, and the auspicious pool of Rudrakarṇa;
the great holy place called Kokila, and likewise the holy place Mahālaya; / Hiraṇyagarbha, Goprekṣa, and the unsurpassed holy place;
Upaśānta, Śiva, and the unsurpassed Vyāghreśvara; / the great holy place Trilocana, and Lokārka called Uttarāhva;
the holy place Kapālamocana, destroying the sin of slaying a brahmin; / the greatly sacred Śukreśvara, and the excellent Ānandapura.
Such are the holy places situated in Vārāṇasī; / it is not possible to describe them in detail even in hundreds of millions of cosmic ages.

3.38.m: Nārada said: / The glorification of Vārāṇasī and the holy places within it, O lord, / have been declared in brief; hear now of other holy places.
Then, having reached Gayā, celibate and composed in mind, / one obtains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice merely by going, O descendant of Bharata.
Where there is the banyan tree named Akṣayyavaṭa, renowned in the three worlds; / whatever is given there to the ancestors becomes imperishable, O lord.
Having bathed in the Mahānadī and satisfied the ancestral spirits and deities, / one attains imperishable worlds and uplifts one's family.
Then one should go to Brahmasaras, frequented by the forest of Brahmā; / one attains the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice, [just as] dawn attains the night.
In that lake, an excellent sacrificial post was erected by Brahmā; / having circumambulated that sacrificial post, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to Dhenuka, renowned in the world; / having stayed for one night, O king, one should donate a sesame cow.
Purified of all sins, one surely goes to the world of the Moon; / there is a sign there, O great king, even today, without doubt:
a tawny cow wanders on the mountain together with her calf; / the footprints of her and her calf are seen even today, O descendant of Bharata.
Having touched water in those footprints, O king of kings, O best of kings, / whatever inauspicious sin exists is destroyed, O descendant of Bharata.
Then one should go to Gṛdhravaṭa, the abode of the trident-bearing god; / bathing there in ashes, having approached the bull-bannered god,
a Brahmin would fulfill a twelve-year vow; / and for the other castes, all sin is destroyed.
Then one should go to the Udyanta mountain, echoing with songs; / for the footprint of Savitṛ is seen there, O bull of the Bharatas.
There a Brahmin of strict vows should perform the twilight devotion; / indeed, by him the twilight devotion will have been observed for twelve years.
And right there is the famous Yonidvāra, O bull of the Bharatas; / having gone there, a person is freed from the constriction of rebirth.
A man who resides in Gayā during both fortnights, the bright and the dark, / purifies his family up to the seventh generation, O king; there is no doubt about this.
Many sons should be desired, so that even one might go to Gayā, / or perform a horse sacrifice, or release a blue bull.
From there, O king, ruler of men, the pilgrim should go to Phalgu; / he obtains the horse sacrifice and attains supreme perfection.
Then, collected in mind, O king of kings, one should go to Dharmapṛṣṭha, / where Dharma always stays, O great king Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having approached Dharma there, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. / Then one should go, O king of kings, to the excellent pilgrimage place of Brahmā.
Having gone there, restrained in vows, one should worship Brahmā; / one obtains the fruit of both the royal consecration and the horse sacrifice, O Bhārata.
From there, the pilgrim should go to Rājagṛha, O ruler of men; / having touched water there, one rejoices like Kakṣīvat.
There, a pure man should first eat the regular offering to the Yakṣiṇī; / by the grace of the Yakṣiṇī, he is freed from the murder of a Brahmin.
Then one should go to Maṇināga and obtain the fruit of a thousand cows; / a person who eats the regular offering of Maṇināga,
if bitten by a venomous serpent, the venom does not affect him, O king; / staying there for one night, he is freed from all sins.
Then one should go to the forest of the divine sage Gautama, O king; / having bathed in the pool of Ahalyā, one attains the supreme state.
Having approached Śrī, O king, one finds supreme fortune. / There is a water reservoir, O knower of dharma, renowned in the three worlds;
one should perform a bath there and obtain a horse sacrifice. / And the well of the royal sage Janaka is worshipped by the gods;
having bathed there, one attains the world of Viṣṇu. / Then one should go to Avināśana, which releases one from all sins;
one obtains a horse sacrifice and goes to the world of Soma. / And having reached the Gaṇḍakī, which contains the waters of all holy places,
one obtains the Vājapeya sacrifice and goes to the world of Sūrya. / Then, O knower of dharma, entering the hermitage of Dhruva,
one rejoices among the Guhyakas, O fortunate one; there is no doubt about this. / Having reached the Karmadā river, frequented by the Siddhas,
one obtains the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice and goes to the world of Soma. / Then, having reached the Viśālā river, famous in the three worlds,
one obtains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world. / Then, having reached Māheśvarīdhārā, O ruler of men,
one obtains a horse sacrifice and delivers his family. / Reaching the lotus pond of the celestials, a pure man
does not suffer a bad rebirth and obtains the Vājapeya sacrifice. / Then a celibate student, collected in mind, should go to Māheśapada.
Having bathed at Māheśvarapada, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. / There, ten million holy places are celebrated, O bull of the Bharatas,
which were taken away by the evil-minded asura in the form of a tortoise, O king of kings, / and recovered by the mighty Viṣṇu, O king.
One should perform a bath there at Tīrthakoṭi, O ruler of men; / one obtains the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Then, O best of men, one should go to the abode of Nārāyaṇa, / where Hari always dwells, ever-present, O Bhārata.
Where Brahmā and the other gods, and the sages rich in austerity, / the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Rudras worship Janārdana,
known as Śālagrāma, belonging to Viṣṇu of wondrous deeds. / Having approached Viṣṇu, the imperishable lord of the three worlds, giver of boons,
one obtains a horse sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. / There is a water reservoir, O knower of dharma, which releases one from all sins;
the four oceans are always present there in that well; / having touched water there, O king of kings, one does not suffer a bad rebirth.
Having approached Mahādeva and the immutable Viṣṇu who grants boons, / one shines like the moon, freed from debts, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Pure and with restrained mind, having touched the water at Jātismara, / having bathed there, one gains memory of previous births; there is no doubt.
Having gone to Vaṭeśvarapura and worshipped Keśava, / through fasting one obtains the desired worlds; there is no doubt.
Then having gone to Vāmana, which destroys all sins, / and bowed to the god Hari, one does not suffer a bad rebirth.
Having gone to the hermitage of Bharata, which releases one from all sins, / one should visit the Kauśikī river there, which destroys great sins.
A person obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. / Then, O knower of dharma, one should go to the excellent Campakāraṇya.
Staying there for one night, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows. / Then, reaching Govinda, the highly esteemed pilgrimage place,
fasting for one night, one obtains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. / Having seen Viśveśvara there, together with the goddess, of great splendor,
one attains the worlds of Mitra and Varuṇa, O bull of the Bharatas; / having fasted there for three nights, one obtains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Reaching Kanyāvasatha, restrained and regulated in diet, / one attains the worlds of Manu Prajāpati, O bull of the Bharatas.
Those who give even a minute gift at Kanyā, O Bhārata— / that, say the sages of strict vows, is imperishable.
Reaching Niṣṭhāvāsa, renowned in the three worlds, / one obtains a horse sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
The men who give gifts at the confluence of the Niṣṭhā, / they go, O tiger among men, to the sorrowless world of Brahmā.
There is the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, famous in the three worlds; / performing a bath there, one obtains the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Reaching Devakūṭa, frequented by hosts of divine sages, / one obtains a horse sacrifice and delivers his family.
Then, O king of kings, one should go to the pool of the sage Kauśika; / there Kauśika Viśvāmitra attained supreme perfection.
Where a wise man dwells for a month on the Kauśikī, O bull of the Bharatas, / whatever merit belongs to a horse sacrifice, he attains it in a month.
Whoever resides at the great pool, the best of all holy places, / does not suffer a bad rebirth, and acquires abundant gold.
Having approached Kumāra, who dwells at Vīrāśrama, / one obtains a horse sacrifice and goes to the world of Śakra.
And reaching the well frequented by the thirty [gods] at Nandinī, / one obtains whatever merit belongs to a human sacrifice, O upholder of the Kurus.
Having bathed at Kālikāsaṃgama, where the Kauśikī and Aruṇā [meet], / a wise person who has fasted for three nights is freed from all sins.
Reaching the Urvaśī pilgrimage place, and likewise Somāśrama, / a wise man, having bathed at Kumbhakarṇāśrama, is honored on earth.

Likewise, bathing at Kokāmukha, chaste and composed,
one attains memory of past lives; this was seen by the ancients.

Reaching the river once, a twice-born achieves his aim;
his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the heavenly realm.

Reaching Ṛṣabhadvīpa, having served the slayer of Krauñca,
and sipping water in the Sarasvatī, he shines seated in an aerial chariot.

There is the Audyānaka holy bath, O great king, frequented by sages;
if one bathes there, one is freed from all sins.

Reaching Brahmatīrtha, the holy place frequented by divine sages,
a man obtains [the fruit of] a Vājapeya sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.

Then, having reached Campā and offered libations in the Bhāgīrathī,
and having approached Daṇḍārpaṇa, he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.

Then one should go to Lāviḍhikā, holy and visited by the meritorious;
he obtains [the fruit of] a Vājapeya sacrifice and is honored, seated in an aerial chariot.
